children.method: Compare the degree of the digit product with the convolution length, and bound each coefficient by the number of digit products it sums.

motivation.text: Cyclic convolution of length $S$ agrees with ordinary polynomial multiplication when the product's degree is below $S$, and the coefficient bound fixes the word width needed to round and carry exactly.

children.claim: The product has degree at most $2\lceil n/b\rceil-2<2n/b\le T/2<S$, so convolution modulo $x^S-1$ has no nonzero wraparound.

quote.quote: Thus convolution modulo $x^S-1$ has no nonzero wraparound.

children.claim: For pairwise coprime $s_1,\dots,s_d$ with prefix products $P_i=\prod_{j<i}s_j$ and $\mu_i=P_i^{-1}\bmod s_i$, the map $\Phi:x\mapsto\prod_ix_i^{\mu_i}$ is a ring isomorphism from $\mathbb C[x]/(x^S-1)$ to $d$-dimensional cyclic convolution sending index $\sum_ja_jP_j$ to coordinates $a_i+\mu_i\sum_{j<i}a_jP_j\bmod s_i$, and on tape $\Phi$, its inverse and the padding cost $O(Tpd^2(1+\ell^\tau))$.
children.method: Check that $\Phi$ respects $x^S=1$ and maps $x$ to an element of order $S$, express the coordinates as a triangular function of the mixed-radix digits, insert padding in one nested scan, reverse the axes, and apply the triangular updates as prefix-controlled cyclic shifts from the last axis to the first.

motivation.text: The Agarwal-Cooley split converts one cyclic convolution into a multidimensional one, and choosing the coordinate powers $\mu_i$ makes the change of order triangular, hence a sequence of controlled cyclic shifts.

quote.quote: The following map uses that algebraic split, with coordinate powers that make the change of order a sequence of controlled cyclic shifts.

children.claim: $\Phi$ respects $x^S=1$, and since each $\mu_i$ is a unit and the $s_i$ are pairwise coprime the image of $x$ has order $S$, so its powers run once through all target monomials and $\Phi$ is an isomorphism preserving cyclic convolution.

quote.quote: Hence $\Phi$ is an isomorphism and preserves cyclic convolution.

children.claim: Index $\sum_ja_jP_j$ goes to $a_i+\mu_i\sum_{j<i}a_jP_j\pmod{s_i}$ because terms with $j>i$ vanish modulo $s_i$ and $\mu_iP_i\equiv1$.

quote.quote: Indeed terms with $j>i$ are divisible by $s_i$, and $\mu_iP_i=1$ modulo $s_i$.

children.claim: After reversing the axes, updating targets $i=d,\dots,1$ uses only original lower-index digits as controls, each update a prefix-controlled rotation of the valid interval $[0,s_i)$.

quote.quote: When target $i$ is updated, none of its lower-index controls has yet changed, so the offset is computed from the original digits $a_j$ required by the formula.

children.claim: Each step is a bijection of the padded box preserving the valid set, so zero padding stays zero, and the inverse subtracts the same offsets for $i=1,\dots,d$.

quote.quote: Consequently zero padding remains zero after every step.

children.claim: Reversing the axes takes $O(d^2)$ adjacent interchanges of $\ell$- or $(\ell-1)$-bit fields, so $\Phi$, its inverse and the padding cost $O(Tpd^2(1+\ell^\tau))$, with offset preparation $o(Tp)$.

quote.quote: Reversing all axes uses $O(d^2)$ such moves. Therefore the map $\Phi$, its inverse, and their padding operations cost \[ O\bigl(Tp\,d^2(1+\ell^\tau)\bigr).

children.method: Identify the last cyclic axis with the negacyclic ring through the twist, note that $\iota$ only changes the shape descriptor, and compute the twists with approximate phases followed by truncation.

motivation.text: A phase twist turns the last cyclic coordinate into a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$ whose negative wrap gives exactly the cyclic wrap once the twist is removed, so the ring convolution computes the complex one.

quote.quote: A phase twist changes the last cyclic coordinate into a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$; its negative wrap gives precisely the original cyclic wrap after the twist is removed.

children.claim: The twist $\Theta:\mathbb C[x_d]/(x_d^r-1)\to\mathcal R_r$, $x_d\mapsto\zeta y$ with $\zeta=e^{\pi i/r}$, is a norm-preserving ring isomorphism multiplying coefficient $k$ by $\zeta^k$, and a product term with $k+l=j+hr$ picks up $\zeta^{k+l}(-1)^h=\zeta^j$.
children.method: Check $(\zeta y)^r=1$, diagonality on the monomial bases, and the sign of each wrapped product term.

motivation.text: Scaling coefficient $k$ by $\zeta^k$ with $\zeta^r=-1$ converts the cyclic relation $x^r=1$ into the negacyclic $y^r=-1$, so the ring in which twiddles are signed shifts can carry the cyclic convolution.

children.salient: The negative wrap from $y^r=-1$ and the factor $\zeta^r=-1$ from the twist cancel exactly, so the twisted negacyclic product is the cyclic one.

children.claim: $\Theta$ is well defined since $(\zeta y)^r=(-1)(-1)=1$, and it is diagonal with nonzero entries $\zeta^k$, hence an isomorphism.

quote.quote: The map \[ \Theta:\mathbb C[x_d]/(x_d^r-1)\longrightarrow\mathcal R, \qquad x_d\longmapsto\zeta y \] is well defined, since $(\zeta y)^r=(-1)(-1)=1$. On the bases $(x_d^k)_{0\le k<r}$ and $(y^k)_{0\le k<r}$ it is diagonal, multiplying coefficient $k$ by the nonzero number $\zeta^k$. It is therefore an isomorphism, with inverse multiplying that coefficient by $\zeta^{-k}$.

children.claim: For $k+l=j+hr$ with $h\in\{0,1\}$ the negacyclic sign $(-1)^h$ and $\zeta^{hr}$ cancel, so untwisting recovers the cyclic coefficient with the correct sign.

quote.quote: Untwisting therefore recovers the cyclic coefficient with the correct sign.

children.claim: Linewise $\Theta$ is $\iota D_+$ with inverse $D_-\iota^{-1}$, all isometries, so $\mathcal M_{\mathbb C}(f,g)=(f*g)/T$ is a bilinear contraction.

quote.quote: The maps $D_\pm$ and $\iota^{\pm1}$ are isometries, so $\mathcal M_{\mathbb C}$ is also a bilinear contraction.

children.claim: With component width $p+2$ both formats concatenate the same words in the same order, so $\iota$ and $\iota^{-1}$ change only the shape descriptor.

quote.quote: Hence $\iota$ and $\iota^{-1}$ change only the shape descriptor and require no payload movement when these component formats agree.
